chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from al-Nadr ibn Suwayd, from Yahya ibn Imran al-Halbi, from Abu Khalid al-Qammam, from Humran, who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'I ask you, may Allah improve you.' He said, 'Yes.'

So I said, 'I was in a certain state, and today I am in another state. I used to enter the land (go out to people) and invite the man, the two, and the woman, and Allah would rescue whom He willed; and today I do not invite anyone.'
He said, 'And there is no harm upon you if you leave between the people and their Lord. So whoever Allah intends to bring out from darkness to light, He brings him out.'
Then he said, 'And there is no harm upon you if you perceive goodness in someone, to introduce something to him with an introduction.'
I said, 'Inform me about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: 'And whoever keeps it alive, it is as though he kept alive all the people.'
He said, 'From burning or drowning.' Then he was silent, then said, 'Its greatest interpretation is that you invite her, so she responds to you.'

key_terms.أَصْلَحَكَ اللَّهُ: May Allah improve you (a common address to the Imam)
key_terms.وَمَنْ أَحْيَاهَا: And whoever keeps it alive (referring to the soul/life)

ai.seo_question: What is the deeper interpretation of 'whoever keeps it alive' in Surah Al-Ma'idah according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Shia concept of *al-amr bi-l-ma'ruf* (enjoining good), clarifying that active invitation is a means but ultimate guidance (*hidayah*) rests with Allah. The Imam’s dual explanation of the verse 'And whoever keeps it alive...' bridges the literal preservation of physical life with the spiritual revival of the believer (*mu'min*) through da'wah, a key exegetical nuance in Shia scholarship. This context validates the transition from active proselytizing to patient waiting, emphasizing that the spiritual 'life' of a soul is the ultimate objective of the caller.
